Khalil’s bravery also resonated beyond Pakistan. Sri Lankan players and officials expressed gratitude for his quick thinking, saying his refusal to stop the bus likely prevented a far greater tragedy.

But Khalil himself rejected the idea that he was seeking fame. Speaking after the attack, he made an emotional appeal against violence and extremism.

“Terrorism has no religion and no humanity,” he said. “Those who do this are enemies of Pakistan, enemies of peace, and enemies of innocent people.”

He urged people to stand together against terrorism, saying that no cause could justify the killing of guests, players, police officers, or civilians.

For many Pakistanis, Khalil became more than a bus driver. He became a reminder that in moments of terror, courage can come from ordinary people asked to do extraordinary things. While the attack left scars on Lahore and on international cricket in Pakistan, his actions remain a powerful story of duty, humanity, and hope amid violence.
